# The Strange Beauty of Waiting

There's something I've been thinking about lately, something I can't quite pin down but that feels important enough to spend time with. It's about waiting—not the annoyed, foot-tapping kind of waiting that happens when you're stuck in traffic or on hold with customer service, but the deeper, slower kind of waiting that comprises so much of human life and seems almost invisible because it's so pervasive.

I think we don't talk about waiting enough. We celebrate arrival, achievement, completion. We obsess over productivity and efficiency, as though the goal is always to minimize the time between desire and satisfaction. But I'm becoming convinced that waiting is where actual life happens, and I wonder if learning to wait well might be one of the most underrated skills we could develop.

Consider childhood. Almost all of it is waiting. You wait to be old enough to stay up late, to go to school, to drive, to leave home. You wait for Christmas morning, for summer vacation, for the girl or boy to notice you. When you're a kid, this waiting often feels excruciating. Time moves differently when you're young—a week feels like a year. But there's also something magical about it. The anticipation itself is its own form of experience. The days before something you're excited about can be just as vivid and real as the event itself.

I remember in middle school, my best friend and I would spend entire lunch periods reading the same comic books series we'd discovered, theorizing about what would happen next, constructing elaborate narratives about where the characters would go. The books came out monthly, which meant roughly thirty days of wondering. Those thirty days were precious in a way I didn't understand at the time. We lived in them. We inhabited the space between episodes like it was a real place.

As we get older, our culture increasingly tells us that this is a waste of time. We can watch the next episode immediately on streaming services. We can skip ahead. We can spoil ourselves if we want. And certainly, some of this technology is genuinely wonderful. But I wonder what we've lost in gaining the ability to skip the waiting.

There's a theory in psychology about flow states—that particular experience of being so absorbed in an activity that time seems to disappear and you're completely engaged with the present moment. What if waiting, real waiting, is its own kind of flow state? What if the quality of our lives might be measured not by how efficiently we get through our days, but by how present we can be in the gaps?

I've noticed this particularly in relationships. When I was younger and newly interested in someone, there were all these small waits that structured the experience. You would have a conversation, and then you'd wait—sometimes anxiously, sometimes deliciously—for the next one. You'd think about what they said. You'd construct possible futures in your mind. You'd write and rewrite messages before sending them, or you wouldn't message at all because that was how you did things.

Now, with instant messaging and constant connectivity, that waiting is almost entirely removed. You can reach someone immediately. You can know almost everything about them before you've had a single conversation. And perhaps this makes modern relationships more efficient, but I'm not sure it makes them deeper. There's something about the space between—the not-knowing, the imagining, the anticipatory daydreaming—that seems to be part of what builds real connection.

I find myself thinking about artists too, and how waiting has historically been central to artistic practice. A painter spends months or years on a single piece, watching it emerge slowly, making small decisions that compound over time. A writer might spend years on a novel, inhabiting the world of their characters, letting it deepen. A musician practices the same piece thousands of times, the waiting between today's practice and tomorrow's, between learning it and mastering it and playing it in front of an audience.

But contemporary culture pushes toward speed in creative work too. Overnight success stories dominate the narrative. We celebrate the prodigy who emerges fully formed, the viral sensation that appears from nowhere. Social media rewards constant output and immediate engagement. There's less space in popular discourse for the artist who worked in obscurity for decades before being recognized.

I wonder if this is a loss. Not everyone can be a overnight success, and even those who are often report that it was hollowing in some way. They hadn't finished becoming who they needed to become. The waiting, it turns out, was doing something important—not preventing their success, but building them into the person capable of handling it meaningfully.

This makes me think about aging, too. Our culture despises aging, fights it viciously, which I think is partly because we've lost any sense that the passage of time might be valuable in itself. We treat getting older as a loss of something, without any sense that we might be gaining anything.

But waiting teaches us things. Patience isn't just patience—it's a way of developing trust in time itself, in the idea that good things can't be rushed and that the process matters as much as the destination. Anticipation teaches us to imagine, to construct possible futures, to hope. Long-term projects teach us about follow-through and commitment. Grief—which is a kind of waiting for acceptance—teaches us about depth and meaning.

I think about people I know who seem genuinely content, and I notice that many of them have developed relationships with waiting. They have gardens, so they wait through seasons. They have partners they've been with for decades, so they know that depth takes time. They have creative practices they've maintained for years. They read books that take a long time, reread them, think about them over years. They don't rush.

And I notice too that they are not bored. If anything, the opposite. There's a richness to their experience precisely because they're not constantly trying to optimize it, to get to the next thing. They're present in what is.

There's something else I've been turning over too, and it's harder to articulate. It's the idea that waiting might be connected to meaning itself. That the meaning of something—how much it matters to us—might be partly a function of how much we've waited for it, thought about it, anticipated it. 

Consider holidays. In cultures where holidays were more anticipated—where they were rare, where you had to wait months for them, where the period before them had specific rituals and preparations—they seem to have meant more. Christmas in earlier centuries, before commercialization, must have felt genuinely transcendent to people because the entire year was in some sense structured around anticipating it. The waiting was half the meaning.

Now we have holidays constantly. There's always something to buy, some next special occasion being marketed to us. And I wonder if this is part of why modern life can feel so meaningless despite having so much—if constant access to everything empties things of their significance.

I've been thinking too about hope, which seems like a form of waiting. Hope is not optimism, exactly. Optimism is a belief that things will turn out well. Hope is something more active—it's a way of maintaining belief in possibility while acknowledging difficulty. It's a verb. You hope; you wait; you trust; you work; and hope sustains you through it. Hope is what allows you to be present with the waiting rather than destroyed by it.

There's this passage from a poem I can't quite remember, something about how "the waiting is all there is." And I think there's truth to that. Even if we get what we're waiting for, we'll just start waiting for something else. Even at the end of our lives, we might be waiting—waiting to know what it all meant, waiting for understanding. 

So the question becomes: can we make peace with the waiting? Can we fall in love with the process rather than remaining fixated on the outcome? Can we understand that waiting well is not wasting time, but using it to build the capacity to live deeply?

I find myself wanting to practice this more intentionally. To put my phone away and wait for someone face-to-face without filling the silence with checking messages. To read a physical book over months instead of devouring it on a screen. To plant seeds and wait for them to grow without checking on them obsessively. To commit to small creative projects without expecting immediate results. To have conversations and not know where they'll go, to be comfortable in not-knowing.

There's a courage in this, I think. It's easier to be constantly stimulated and distracted than to be truly present with waiting. There's an anxiety in it too—the fear that we'll wait for the wrong thing, or that while we're waiting, we're missing something else. But I'm starting to think that's okay, that some anxiety is the price of depth.

And maybe the real insight is this: we are all waiting, always, whether we acknowledge it or not. We're waiting for the future to arrive, and the future will never arrive in the way we imagine. By the time it gets here, it will be the present, which is always much more ordinary and complicated and mixed than we anticipated. So the waiting is what we actually have. It's the real thing. Everything else is what we think should be real, but the waiting—the living in anticipation and process and not-knowing—that's where we actually exist.

I want to close by saying something about gratitude, because I think it's connected. When we wait for something, and we're present in the waiting, we often approach what we receive with more gratitude. We notice it more. We appreciate it more. We see it not as inevitable, but as a gift, as something that took time and effort and luck to attain. This seems like another reason that our culture's obsession with speed might be impoverishing us—not just removing the joy of anticipation, but removing the gratitude that comes after.

I don't have a neat conclusion to offer here. I'm still thinking about these things, still learning to wait better. But I wanted to write about waiting because it's on my mind and it seems important and because I think we'd do well to talk about it more. To defend it. To recognize waiting not as wasted time but as the texture of a meaningful life. To remember that sometimes the best things in life are the ones that take the longest, cost the most, demand the most patience. And to somehow find peace and even beauty in that eternal present-tense of anticipation, where we're always moving toward something and never quite arriving, and somehow that's exactly as it should be.
